clue.text: Two elements in strongliquor…

parts.note: fire is one of the four classical elements
water is another of the four classical elements

explanation.surface: Two chemical elements found in a powerful spirit, the sentence trailing on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs this clue on into 6 across, which names the apparatus that makes the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Firewater is an informal term for strong alcoholic spirits such as whisky or rum.

clue.text: Newspaper accepts honour for a feature

indicators.note: accepts means the newspaper takes the honour inside itself

parts.note: FT is the Financial Times, a British newspaper
in bridge the ace is one of the honour cards

explanation.surface: A newspaper accepts an award as the subject of a feature article.
explanation.walkthrough: 'honour' looks like a medal but is a card term.
explanation.definitionFit: A facet is an aspect or feature of something.

clue.text: The application of reason, changing a liaison into art

indicators.note: changing signals that the following letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram letters
taken as written as anagram letters
taken as written as anagram letters

explanation.surface: Reason is applied by turning a love affair into a work of art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' looks like a link but is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Rationalisation is making something logical by applying reason to it.

clue.text: Any power supply does for Arsenal

indicators.note: supply is read as the adverb 'supplely', so the letters bend into a new order

parts.note: taken as written as anagram letters

explanation.surface: Any source of power will do for Arsenal football club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arsenal' suggests the London football club but means a store of arms.
explanation.definitionFit: An arsenal is a stock of arms, which is weaponry.

clue.text: Care for shoes in box, possibly

definitions.meaning: a shaped block put inside footwear to keep its form
box is one example of a woody plant species

explanation.definitionFit: A shoe tree keeps shoes in shape, and box is an example of a tree.

clue.text: With injection of metallic element double the brains

indicators.note: injection of means one piece is put into the other

parts.note: a ringer is a double, someone who looks just like another
lead is a metallic element

explanation.surface: A lookalike given a metal injection takes on all the cleverness.
explanation.definitionFit: The brains behind a scheme is its organiser or leader.

clue.text: …produced by this even now

definitions.meaning: read with 1 across, the drink is produced by a distilling apparatus
as in 'it is even now raining': up to this moment

explanation.definitionFit: A still is the distilling apparatus that makes spirits, and 'still' as an adverb means as yet, even now.

clue.text: Informant showing resentment to the church

parts.note: sour feeling is resentment; sour as a noun
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A grudging informer reports to the church.
explanation.definitionFit: A source is someone who supplies information, an informant.

clue.text: Put away frequently, I'm contrite finally almost too late

parts.note: in the nick is British slang for in prison, put away
oft is an old word for frequently
taken as written

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of contrite

explanation.surface: Someone jailed again and again repents only at the very end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the nick' is British slang for prison.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nick of time means at the last moment, just before it is too late.

clue.text: Churchman, one who will guide you round Scottish port

indicators.note: round places the guide's word around the port

parts.note: a leader guides others
Ayr is a port on the west coast of Scotland

explanation.surface: A clergyman acts as your guide on a tour of a Scottish harbour.
explanation.definitionFit: A lay reader is a layperson licensed to conduct certain church services.

clue.text: Surplice, for instance, sent back by river to test small business

parts.note: a cotta is a short surplice worn by clergy and choristers

indicators.note: sent back tells us to read the abbreviation for 'for instance' from right to left

parts.note: EG is the abbreviation for exempli gratia, 'for instance'
the Indus is a great river of Pakistan
to try is to test

explanation.surface: A choir garment is returned by the river to test some small enterprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent back' turns EG into GE. 'by' and 'to' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A cottage industry is a small business, originally one run from home.

clue.text: Excessively short skirt, by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it says the skirt's name is said aloud, giving a word that is pronounced the same

parts.note: a tutu is a ballet dancer's short stiff skirt

explanation.surface: A remark that a skirt is scandalously short, judged by how it sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Too-too is an old-fashioned affected expression meaning excessively or extremely.

clue.text: Mouse, live, taken outside by servant

indicators.note: taken outside by places the two letters for 'live' around the servant's word

parts.note: to be is to live or exist
a lackey is a liveried servant

explanation.surface: A servant carries a living mouse out of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mouse' looks like the rodent but is slang for a bruised eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Mouse is slang for a bruise around the eye, a shiner.

clue.text: Changing colours in a play

indicators.note: changing signals that the following letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram letters

explanation.surface: A theatre changes its colour scheme for a production.
explanation.definitionFit: Coriolanus is a tragedy by Shakespeare.

clue.text: Convener, one daily employed

indicators.note: employed is read as 'used in', so the numeral goes inside the cleaner's title

parts.note: a daily is a British cleaner who comes in each day, a charwoman
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A meeting's organiser is one of the cleaners on the payroll.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'daily' is British usage for a domestic cleaner.
explanation.definitionFit: The convener of a meeting presides over it, which is a chairperson's role.

clue.text: Lock up prisoner, 14

parts.note: a con is a convict, a prisoner
14 across is a kind, and a strain is a kind or breed

explanation.surface: Lock up a convict of a certain sort.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to 14 across, whose answer means type; STRAIN is a synonym of it.
explanation.definitionFit: To constrain someone can mean to confine or restrict them, as in locking up.

clue.text: Stamp showing King's head, produced by India

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, here of King's

explanation.surface: A postage stamp bearing the King's head, issued in India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stamp' looks like postage but means a type or sort, as in 'a man of that stamp'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamp in the sense of character or sort is a synonym of kind.

clue.text: Scrap page added to feature

parts.note: a feature in a newspaper is an article

explanation.surface: A discarded page is added to a magazine feature.
explanation.definitionFit: A particle is a tiny fragment, a scrap.

clue.text: Fasten collar

definitions.meaning: to fix something in place with a metal spike
to collar someone is to catch or arrest them

explanation.definitionFit: To nail is both to fix with a spike and, informally, to catch or arrest a person.

clue.text: At every step, he may collect ashes for religious rite

definitions.text: At every step, he may collect ashes for religious rite

parts.words: At every step, he may collect ashes for religious rite
parts.note: a person walking barefoot over embers might literally pick up ashes on each foot during a ceremony

explanation.surface: A celebrant gathers ashes step by step during a sacred ceremony.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who walks barefoot over hot coals, often as part of a religious ceremony, would tread ashes at every step.

clue.text: See friend at first somewhat indistinctly

indicators.note: at first puts the friend in front of the see

parts.note: a pal is a friend
Ely is a cathedral city and bishop's see in Cambridgeshire

explanation.surface: Seeing a friend at first only vaguely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like a verb but is a bishop's diocese.
explanation.definitionFit: To shine palely is to shine faintly, rather indistinctly.

clue.text: Over the top, flat out — a blunder

indicators.note: blunder is read as a verb, the letters stumbling into a new order

parts.note: taken as written as anagram letters

explanation.surface: Someone races flat out, overdoing it, and makes a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of FLAT OUT A, signalled by 'blunder', gives the answer; 'a blunder' looks like a definition of FAULT but is not.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something to a fault means to excess, which is going over the top.

clue.text: County provides help for crooks

definitions.meaning: The short form of Staffordshire, an English county in the Midlands
walking sticks or poles support those who bend, and a shepherd's crook is itself a staff

explanation.definitionFit: Staffs abbreviates Staffordshire, and staffs are sticks that support walkers or shepherds' crooks.

clue.text: A great many show regret over time

indicators.note: over means the regret word sits above time in this down entry

parts.note: to sigh is to show regret

explanation.surface: A large crowd expresses sorrow about the passing of time.
explanation.definitionFit: A sight, in informal British use, means a great deal, as in 'a sight better'.

clue.text: A country's upset by predatory bird

indicators.note: upset, in a down entry, turns the joined pieces upside down

parts.note: the UK's, the country's, gives UK plus S

explanation.surface: A nation is disturbed by a bird of prey.
explanation.definitionFit: The skua is a seabird that robs and preys on other birds.

clue.text: Full of vigour, I laid knave out (clubs), then a higher card

indicators.note: out signals that the letters are disordered or put out of place

parts.note: taken as written as anagram letters
C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
the king ranks just above the knave in a suit

explanation.surface: A card player lays down a knave of clubs and then tops it with a king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges I LAID KNAVE into ALIVEANDKI.
explanation.definitionFit: Alive and kicking is an idiom for being healthy and active, full of vigour.

clue.text: Two names borne by no childminder

indicators.note: borne by means carried inside the word for no

parts.note: nay is an old word for no
N is the abbreviation for name, and two of them give NN

explanation.surface: A carer with two names who is supported by no one.
explanation.definitionFit: A nanny is a person employed to look after children.

clue.text: Having driven around, got together at return for presentation

indicators.note: around puts the word for 'driven' outside the reversed letters

parts.note: having driven someone mad is having sent them so

indicators.note: return turns the joined words for 'got together' and 'at' backwards

parts.note: met means got together

explanation.surface: After a drive round, people met up again for a talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having driven' as SENT is the sense of driving someone mad; 'return' turns 'got together at' backwards, and 'around' wraps the result.
explanation.definitionFit: A statement is a formal presentation of facts or views.
